title: How Resistance Genes Travel
topic: antibiotic resistance and horizontal gene transfer
paragraphs: Penicillin reached general clinical use in the early 1940s, and within a decade hospitals were reporting infections that shrugged it off.
That reversal set the pattern for nearly every antibiotic since: a compound arrives, works spectacularly, and then loses ground, sometimes within years.
The usual explanation, that bacteria evolve quickly because they divide quickly, is true as far as it goes and incomplete in a way that matters for how the problem is managed.
The familiar account runs through mutation and selection.
A bacterium copying its chromosome makes occasional errors; most are harmful or meaningless, but a few alter a drug's target, the envelope's permeability, or a pump that expels foreign molecules.
In the presence of the drug, that cell leaves more descendants than its neighbors.
Because a population in rich medium can double every twenty minutes, a rare variant can dominate within days.
This is ordinary vertical descent: the gene passes from parent to offspring and the lineage grows.
Vertical descent alone, though, cannot account for what clinicians actually see.
Resistance to a new drug often appears in several unrelated species at once, in the same ward or stretch of river, carrying the same gene with the same sequence.
Independent mutation does not produce identical answers in lineages that have not shared an ancestor for hundreds of millions of years.
Something is moving the gene itself.
Bacteria pass genes sideways as well as down, a process called horizontal gene transfer.
Three routes do most of the work.
In conjugation, a donor carrying a conjugative plasmid extends a pilus that binds a recipient and draws the cells into direct contact.
A relaxase enzyme then nicks one strand of the plasmid at a sequence called the origin of transfer, and that single strand is threaded through a channel into the recipient.
Both cells synthesize the complementary strand, and the recipient becomes a donor in its own right.
These plasmids are circular DNA molecules separate from the chromosome, replicating on their own schedule.
A single plasmid may carry a dozen resistance determinants plus genes for metal tolerance, virulence, and its own transfer machinery.
Some live within one genus; others are far less particular, establishing themselves in hosts as distantly related as Escherichia and Pseudomonas.
A cell that receives one acquires an entire package at once, so a susceptible strain can become multidrug resistant with no intermediate stage.
The second route requires no contact at all.
Dying bacteria release DNA into their surroundings, and some species can take that naked DNA across the envelope and recombine it into their own chromosome.
The capacity is called competence, and in several species it switches on under stress or at a certain population density.
The third route conscripts viruses.
Bacteriophages package their genome into new particles, and occasionally the machinery takes a piece of host DNA by mistake.
When such a particle infects another cell, it injects bacterial genes instead of viral ones.
Generalized transduction moves more or less any fragment of the host chromosome; specialized transduction moves the segments that lie alongside a phage's integration site.
Neither is efficient per particle, but phages are so abundant in seawater and sediment that rare events become routine.
Arriving is not the same as being used.
A gene that lands in a new cell without a promoter in front of it sits inert.
Integrons solve that problem, and they explain how resistance accumulates rather than merely appears.
An integron is a genetic filing system: an integrase gene, a recombination site for new material, and a single promoter aimed at that site.
Incoming gene cassettes, small circular units carrying one gene apiece, are cut in under the resident promoter.
A fresh cassette inserts nearest the promoter, so the most recent addition is expressed most strongly, while older ones sit further back in the array.
Integrons themselves are not mobile, but they ride on things that are.
Class 1 integrons in particular sit inside transposons that hop onto plasmids, and those plasmids conjugate.
Arrays holding five or six cassettes are common in clinical isolates.
This raises an obvious question: where do the genes come from in the first place?
The intuitive answer, that antibiotics created them, is simply wrong.

Bacteria from a deep cave chamber in New Mexico, cut off from the surface for something on the order of four million years, carry resistance to multiple modern drug classes, including compounds first made in a laboratory.
DNA from permafrost tens of thousands of years old contains recognizable genes for enzymes that destroy penicillin type drugs.
The reason is not mysterious: many antibiotic scaffolds in clinical use came from soil microbes, which must protect themselves from what they make.
The standing pool of such genes in soil and gut communities is large enough to have earned a name, the resistome, and it is ancient.
The antibiotic era did not invent resistance.

It applied intense selection to a reservoir that was already there, and it rearranged the contents of that reservoir, pulling genes out of soil chromosomes, onto plasmids, and into the species that infect people.
This distinction, between resistance arising and resistance spreading, is the one most often collapsed in public discussion, and collapsing it leads to bad predictions.
Arising is chemistry and chance, and has gone on for as long as microbes have made antibiotics.
Spreading is a matter of ecology: how much drug is present, how often cells meet, how mobile the element is, and how many hosts it tolerates.
Only the second of those is something human behavior can push on.
Hospitals, feedlots, and sewage systems are not laboratories where resistance is invented but mixing vessels where it is concentrated and moved.
There is a tempting corollary: resistance is supposed to be costly.
A pump that expels molecules burns energy, an altered ribosome may translate less efficiently, and a plasmid adds DNA that must be copied at every division.
In the absence of the drug, a resistant cell should therefore fall behind a susceptible one, and resistance should drain out of a population once prescribing stops.
The reasoning is sound and the premise is often true.
The conclusion, unfortunately, does not follow as reliably as it should.
Several things blunt it.
Compensatory mutations elsewhere in the genome restore the lost efficiency while leaving the resistance gene intact, so the cost can shrink toward nothing within a few hundred generations.

Co-selection links otherwise independent determinants: a plasmid carrying resistance to an abandoned drug may also carry resistance to one still in use, so ordinary practice keeps selecting for the whole package.
Some plasmids carry toxin antitoxin systems, pairing a durable toxin with a short lived antidote, so a daughter cell that fails to inherit the plasmid poisons itself.
And some resistance genes appear to cost very little from the beginning.
The empirical record matches that picture rather than the tidy one.
Where national programs have sharply and durably cut a whole drug class, resistance in some target organisms has declined measurably.
Elsewhere, the same kind of restriction has produced years of flat numbers.
A gene that has become fixed in a population, with its cost paid down and its carriage tied to other advantages, does not vanish because prescribing habits change.
Reversal happens, but it is slow, partial, and organism specific, and no one should plan around it as though it were a wall switch.
None of this argues against stewardship.
It argues for a more honest version of it.
If the aim is to restore an earlier state, stewardship will look like failure.

If the aim is to slow the movement of genes that already exist, then the tools follow: diagnostics that separate bacterial from viral illness before prescribing, narrow agents rather than broad ones, courses no longer than necessary, infection control that keeps resistant strains from new hosts, and sanitation that keeps gut plasmids out of the water supply.
These measures buy time rather than turning back the clock, and time is what a slow drug development pipeline needs most.
Treating resistance as a contaminant to be cleaned up misreads what it is.
It is a standing feature of microbial life, older than medicine by a wide margin, and the realistic goal is to manage the traffic rather than to clear the road.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happens immediately after the relaxase nicks one strand of a conjugative plasmid?
choices: One strand of the plasmid passes into the recipient through a channel
The recipient degrades the incoming DNA before replication begins
The pilus retracts and the donor permanently loses its plasmid
The plasmid inserts itself into the recipient chromosome at the origin of transfer site
A virus particle packages the plasmid and carries it across

proof.quote: that single strand is threaded through a channel into the recipient

questions.why: Paragraph 4 walks through conjugation in order: contact, pilus, relaxase nick at the origin of transfer, then the single nicked strand threaded through a channel into the recipient. The answer is the next step in that sequence.
distractorNotes: The passage never mentions the recipient destroying incoming DNA during conjugation; it says the recipient builds the complementary strand and becomes a donor itself.
The passage says the recipient becomes a donor in its own right, which means the donor keeps a copy rather than losing the plasmid.
The origin of transfer is where the relaxase cuts, not a site where the plasmid integrates into the chromosome; plasmids in this passage replicate separately from the chromosome.
Packaging into a virus particle is transduction, described in paragraph 7, not conjugation.

questions.stem: The passage indicates that the gene cassette most recently added to an integron is
choices: silenced until the older cassettes are excised
placed farthest from the promoter and expressed weakly
expressed most strongly because it sits closest to the promoter
copied onto a separate plasmid before any of it can be expressed
given a dedicated promoter of its own by the integrase

proof.quote: A fresh cassette inserts nearest the promoter
the most recent addition is expressed most strongly

questions.why: Paragraph 8 explains that a fresh cassette inserts nearest the single resident promoter, so the newest arrival is expressed most strongly and older cassettes sit further back in the array.
distractorNotes: Nothing in the passage requires older cassettes to be removed; they simply sit further back and are expressed less strongly.
This reverses the arrangement in paragraph 8. The newest cassette goes nearest the promoter, and the older ones are the ones sitting further away.
The passage says cassettes are filed into the integron and expressed there. Movement onto a plasmid happens to the whole integron, and it is not a requirement for expression.
The point of the integron is that one shared promoter serves the array. A cassette arrives without a promoter of its own, which is exactly the problem integrons solve.

questions.stem: As the passage describes them, toxin antitoxin systems on a plasmid work because
choices: the toxin kills neighboring susceptible cells and clears competitors from the surrounding population
the toxin speeds the transfer of the plasmid into new hosts
the system lowers the energy cost of carrying the plasmid
the toxin destroys any competing plasmid that enters the cell
the antidote is short lived, so a cell losing the plasmid dies

proof.quote: a durable toxin with a short lived antidote
a daughter cell that fails to inherit the plasmid poisons itself

questions.why: Paragraph 14 pairs a durable toxin with a short lived antidote. When a daughter cell fails to inherit the plasmid, the antidote disappears first and the lingering toxin kills that cell, which is why the plasmid is hard to shed.
distractorNotes: The passage describes the toxin acting on the cell that lost the plasmid, not on neighboring cells.
Moving a plasmid into new hosts is the work of the conjugation machinery in paragraph 4; paragraph 14 ties the toxin only to what happens in a cell that loses the plasmid.
Paragraph 13 states that a plasmid adds DNA that must be copied at every division, so it adds cost rather than lowering it. Compensatory mutations, not toxin systems, are what reduce cost here.
Nothing in the passage describes the toxin attacking other plasmids; the target is the cell that failed to inherit this one.

questions.stem: According to the passage, specialized transduction moves
choices: any fragment of the host chromosome, with roughly equal probability for each
the chromosomal segments lying next to where the phage integrates
only plasmids that carry resistance cassettes
naked DNA released into the surroundings by cells that have died
the phage genome alone, with no bacterial DNA

proof.quote: specialized transduction moves the segments that lie alongside a phage's integration site

questions.why: Paragraph 7 draws the contrast directly: generalized transduction moves more or less any fragment, while specialized transduction moves the segments that lie alongside a phage's integration site.
distractorNotes: That describes generalized transduction, which the passage names in the same sentence as the contrast.
Plasmids move by conjugation in paragraph 4. The passage does not restrict transduction to plasmids.
Uptake of naked DNA from the surroundings is competence, described in paragraph 6.
If only the phage genome moved, no bacterial gene would travel at all, and the passage is explaining how bacterial genes ride along.

questions.stem: Which of the following is offered in the passage as evidence that resistance genes existed before the antibiotic era?
choices: Soil bacteria shed their resistance genes within a few generations once antibiotics are withdrawn
Clinical isolates commonly carry integrons holding five or six cassettes
Bacterial populations in rich medium can double every twenty minutes
Cave bacteria sealed off for millions of years resist several modern drug classes
Permafrost bacteria grow faster than bacteria taken from the surface

proof.quote: cut off from the surface for something on the order of four million years
carry resistance to multiple modern drug classes

questions.why: Paragraph 10 gives two pieces of evidence, and this is one of them: bacteria from a New Mexico cave chamber cut off from the surface for roughly four million years resist multiple modern drug classes.
distractorNotes: The passage argues the opposite in paragraphs 13 through 15. Resistance often persists after a drug is withdrawn rather than disappearing quickly.
That detail is true and appears in paragraph 9, but it describes how much resistance accumulates in current clinical strains, not how old resistance is.
That figure comes from paragraph 2 and explains how fast a variant can spread, which is a different question.
The passage mentions permafrost DNA carrying penicillin destroying enzyme genes, not anything about growth rates.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 11, "reservoir" most nearly means
choices: a tank constructed to hold water for later use
a species that carries a pathogen without ever becoming ill from it
an existing supply of genes that selection can draw from
a laboratory collection of preserved bacterial strains
a barrier that keeps genes from moving between species

proof.quote: applied intense selection to a reservoir that was already there
The standing pool of such genes in soil and gut communities

questions.why: Paragraph 11 calls the standing pool of resistance genes in soil and gut communities the resistome and says the antibiotic era applied selection to a reservoir that was already there. The word names a pre existing supply, not a container.
distractorNotes: This is the everyday dictionary sense. Nothing is being stored as water here, and the passage is talking about genes in living communities.
This is a real biological use of the word in the study of infection, but the passage is describing a pool of genes, not a host species that stays healthy.
The pool described sits in soil and gut communities in the wild, not in a curated laboratory collection.
The paragraph says the era pulled genes out of soil chromosomes and into human pathogens, so the reservoir is a source of movement, not a barrier against it.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 15, "fixed" most nearly means
choices: repaired after having been damaged
held at a single location on the chromosome
set in advance by the prescribing physician
established across a population and not easily lost
attached permanently to a plasmid so that it cannot be shed

proof.quote: A gene that has become fixed in a population
does not vanish because prescribing habits change

questions.why: Paragraph 15 says a gene that has become fixed in a population, with its cost paid down, does not vanish when prescribing habits change. The word describes a gene that has become a settled part of the population.
distractorNotes: This is the most common everyday meaning, but the sentence is about a gene spreading through a population, not about something broken being mended.
This confuses the gene's position in a genome with its frequency in a population, which is what the sentence is tracking.
The paragraph is about what happens in bacterial populations regardless of prescribing, and prescribing habits are named as the thing that changes without dislodging the gene.
Plasmid carriage is one reason a gene persists, described in paragraph 14, but the sentence is about the gene's standing in the population as a whole, not its physical attachment.

questions.stem: The passage implies that if resistance genes moved only from parent to offspring, then
choices: resistance would appear far sooner after a drug is introduced
plasmids would carry more cassettes than they currently do
different lineages would be expected to arrive at different genetic solutions
resistance would still be expected to appear as the same sequence in distant species
resistance would be confined to the species that manufacture antibiotics

proof.quote: Independent mutation does not produce identical answers in lineages
carrying the same gene with the same sequence
Something is moving the gene itself.

questions.why: Paragraph 3 argues that independent mutation cannot produce identical answers in unrelated lineages, which is why the shared sequence points to transfer. Turn that around and vertical descent alone would leave each lineage with its own separate solution.
distractorNotes: Nothing suggests vertical descent alone would be faster. Paragraph 5 notes that transfer can deliver a whole package at once, which is the faster route.
Cassette counts come from paragraph 9 and depend on integrons capturing incoming genes, which is horizontal movement, not vertical descent.
This is exactly the observation paragraph 3 says vertical descent cannot explain, which is why the author concludes the gene itself is moving.
Paragraph 10 says producer organisms protect themselves, but the passage never claims resistance would be limited to them without transfer.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, what can be inferred about a resistance gene that carries almost no fitness cost?
choices: It must have arrived by transduction rather than by conjugation or by transformation
It requires a compensatory mutation before it can be expressed at all
It will spread in hospital wards but not in soil communities
It cannot be carried on a plasmid alongside other resistance genes
Withdrawing the drug would be an unusually weak way to reduce it

proof.quote: some resistance genes appear to cost very little from the beginning
resistance should drain out of a population once prescribing stops
with its cost paid down

questions.why: Paragraphs 13 and 14 hang the whole case for reversal on the idea that resistance is costly, and paragraph 14 lists low cost genes as one reason withdrawal disappoints. If there is little cost to escape, removing the drug removes little pressure against the gene.
distractorNotes: Cost has nothing to do with which of the three transfer routes delivered the gene; the passage never links the two.
Compensatory mutations reduce an existing cost, as paragraph 14 says. A gene that already costs little has no need of one, and the passage never ties them to expression.
The passage places resistance genes in soil communities from the start, in paragraphs 10 and 11, so this contradicts the text.
Paragraph 5 describes plasmids carrying a dozen determinants at once, and nothing excludes a low cost gene from riding along.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the central point of the passage?
choices: Agricultural antibiotic use is the single cause of resistance in human infections, and restricting it would solve the problem
Resistance genes are ancient and spread chiefly by gene transfer, so stewardship should aim at slowing that spread rather than reversing it
Because bacteria divide quickly, mutation and selection within single lineages account for nearly all the resistance clinicians encounter
Conjugation, transformation, and transduction are the three routes of horizontal gene transfer, and each contributes to the spread of resistance
Since resistance cannot be reversed once it appears, the only realistic response is to keep developing new antibiotics faster than the old ones fail

proof.quote: and it is ancient
rearranged the contents of that reservoir
slow the movement of genes that already exist
manage the traffic rather than to clear the road

questions.why: The passage moves from a puzzle about speed, through the transfer mechanisms, to the evidence that resistance is ancient, and lands in paragraphs 15 and 16 on stewardship as a way to slow movement rather than restore an earlier state. That arc is the main idea.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 12 names feedlots as one mixing vessel among several, alongside hospitals and sewage, so the passage never makes agriculture the single cause.
Paragraph 1 calls this explanation true as far as it goes but incomplete, and paragraph 3 says it cannot account for what clinicians see.
This is accurate and occupies several paragraphs, but it is the machinery the argument uses, not the conclusion the passage reaches.
Paragraph 15 says reversal does happen, though slowly and partially, and paragraph 16 endorses stewardship rather than abandoning it for new drugs.

questions.stem: The author's main purpose in describing the cave bacteria and the permafrost DNA is
choices: to correct the assumption that resistance genes arose in the antibiotic era
to show that resistance is more severe in natural settings than it is in hospitals
to argue that soil bacteria should be mined for the next generation of drugs
to explain how integrons capture and file incoming gene cassettes
to warn that thawing permafrost will release new pathogens

proof.quote: where do the genes come from in the first place
that antibiotics created them, is simply wrong

questions.why: Paragraph 10 opens by asking where the genes come from and says flatly that the intuitive answer, that antibiotics created them, is wrong. The cave and the permafrost are the evidence brought in to overturn that assumption.
distractorNotes: The passage does not compare severity between settings. Paragraph 12 calls hospitals and feedlots mixing vessels, which is about concentration, not severity.
Paragraph 10 notes that many antibiotic scaffolds came from soil microbes, but that is background, not a proposal for drug discovery.
Integrons are explained in paragraph 8, several paragraphs earlier, and for a different reason.
Nothing in the passage predicts a release of pathogens from thawing. The permafrost appears only as a record of ancient DNA.

questions.stem: Which best describes the relationship between paragraph 13 and paragraph 14?
choices: Paragraph 13 gives a single example and paragraph 14 generalizes from it to a broader rule
Both paragraphs describe the same mechanism from two different angles
Paragraph 13 raises a question that paragraph 14 declines to answer
Paragraph 14 supplies fresh experimental evidence for the claim in paragraph 13
Paragraph 13 builds a sound expectation and paragraph 14 explains why it often fails

proof.quote: resistance should drain out of a population once prescribing stops
does not follow as reliably as it should
Several things blunt it.

questions.why: Paragraph 13 builds the fitness cost argument and grants that its reasoning is sound, then says the conclusion does not follow reliably. Paragraph 14 opens with the phrase about what blunts it and lists the specific mechanisms that do so.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 13 presents a general argument rather than a single example, and paragraph 14 narrows to specific mechanisms rather than widening.
The two paragraphs describe opposing forces, not one mechanism seen twice.
Paragraph 14 answers the question paragraph 13 leaves open, in four distinct ways.
Paragraph 14 offers mechanisms that undercut the expectation, not evidence that supports it. The empirical record arrives in paragraph 15.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the common habit of treating resistance arising and resistance spreading as one thing is best described as
choices: amused by it
indifferent, since the distinction makes no practical difference to patients
approving, since simplification helps public understanding
critical, because merging the two leads to unreliable expectations
alarmed, predicting an imminent epidemic because of the confusion

proof.quote: collapsing it leads to bad predictions

questions.why: Paragraph 12 says the distinction is the one most often collapsed in public discussion and that collapsing it leads to bad predictions. That is measured criticism, not amusement or panic.
distractorNotes: There is no humor in the paragraph. The language is corrective and plainly serious.
The paragraph argues the opposite, that the distinction determines what human action can actually change.
The author treats the simplification as a source of bad predictions, so approval is the reverse of the stance taken.
The tone is analytical rather than alarmed, and the passage makes no prediction of an imminent epidemic.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward antibiotic stewardship is best described as
choices: skeptical that stewardship is worth the effort it requires
supportive, provided its goal is understood as slowing spread rather than reversing it
confident that strict stewardship will restore susceptibility within about a decade
neutral, presenting stewardship without offering any evaluation of it
dismissive of diagnostics and infection control as minor measures next to new drug development

proof.quote: None of this argues against stewardship.
It argues for a more honest version of it.
slow the movement of genes that already exist

questions.why: Paragraph 16 states outright that none of this argues against stewardship and that it argues for a more honest version, then says the measures buy time rather than turning back the clock. That is support with a corrected goal.
distractorNotes: The paragraph opens by denying exactly this reading and goes on to list the tools stewardship should use.
Paragraph 15 says reversal is slow, partial, and organism specific, which rules out confidence in a decade long restoration.
The author evaluates stewardship directly, calling for a more honest version of it and naming which aims will and will not work.
Diagnostics and infection control head the author's own list of tools, and new drug development is presented as needing the time stewardship buys.

questions.stem: The passage supports all of the following statements EXCEPT:
choices: Some plasmids can establish themselves in distantly related host genera
A phage particle can inject bacterial DNA into a new host cell
Competence allows a cell to take up DNA released into its surroundings by dying bacteria
Integrons move between cells on their own, without help from other elements
Compensatory mutations can reduce the cost of carrying a resistance gene

proof.quote: Integrons themselves are not mobile, but they ride on things that are.
hosts as distantly related as Escherichia and Pseudomonas
it injects bacterial genes instead of viral ones
take that naked DNA across the envelope
The capacity is called competence
the cost can shrink toward nothing within a few hundred generations

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says plainly that integrons themselves are not mobile and that they ride on transposons which hop onto plasmids. The other four statements each restate something the passage asserts.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 5 says some plasmids establish themselves in hosts as distantly related as Escherichia and Pseudomonas, so this is supported.
Paragraph 7 describes a particle that injects bacterial genes instead of viral ones, so this is supported.
Paragraph 6 defines competence as the capacity to take up naked DNA released by dying bacteria, so this is supported.
Paragraph 14 says compensatory mutations restore lost efficiency so the cost shrinks toward nothing, so this is supported.

questions.stem: A reader who wants to know how a resistance gene that arrives without a promoter can still be switched on should look in the paragraph that discusses
choices: the integron and its gene cassettes
the steps of conjugation and the origin of transfer
the cave and permafrost evidence
the difference between resistance arising and resistance spreading
the stewardship measures near the end

proof.quote: without a promoter in front of it sits inert
Integrons solve that problem

questions.why: Paragraph 8 raises exactly that problem, saying a gene that lands without a promoter sits inert, and then presents the integron with its single shared promoter as the solution.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 4 explains how DNA physically gets into a new cell, which is the step before the expression problem arises.
Paragraph 10 addresses the age and origin of resistance genes, not how an arriving gene is expressed.
Paragraph 12 separates two processes conceptually and does not deal with promoters.
Paragraph 16 lists practical measures and says nothing about gene expression.
